```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)

jobs_raw <- read_csv("AI Job Market Dataset.csv")

names(jobs_raw)
dim(jobs_raw)
head(jobs_raw)
```

## Data Preparation and Database Construction

The dataset contains 10,345 job postings and five technical skill indicators. I will organize these into normalized relational tables to separate job information from skill information.

```{r}
skill_columns <- c(
  "skills_python",
  "skills_sql",
  "skills_ml",
  "skills_deep_learning",
  "skills_cloud"
)

skill_values <- jobs_raw |>
  select(job_id, all_of(skill_columns)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(skill_columns),
    names_to = "skill_name",
    values_to = "required"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    skill_name = recode(
      skill_name,
      skills_python = "Python",
      skills_sql = "SQL",
      skills_ml = "Machine Learning",
      skills_deep_learning = "Deep Learning",
      skills_cloud = "Cloud Computing"
    )
  )

head(skill_values, 10)
```

## Relational Database

To organize the job-posting data, I created three normalized tables: jobs, skills, and job_skills. This avoids repeating skill names in every job record and creates a many-to-many relationship between jobs and skills.

```{r}
# Create job information table
jobs <- jobs_raw |>
  select(-all_of(skill_columns)) |>
  distinct(job_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Create a unique table for the five skills
skills <- tibble(
  skill_id = 1:5,
  skill_name = c(
    "Python",
    "SQL",
    "Machine Learning",
    "Deep Learning",
    "Cloud Computing"
  )
)

# Connect each job to its required skills
job_skills <- skill_values |>
  filter(required == 1) |>
  left_join(skills, by = "skill_name") |>
  select(job_id, skill_id) |>
  distinct()

# Create SQLite database in memory
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")

# Store the three normalized tables
dbWriteTable(con, "jobs", jobs, overwrite = TRUE)
dbWriteTable(con, "skills", skills, overwrite = TRUE)
dbWriteTable(con, "job_skills", job_skills, overwrite = TRUE)

# Verify database tables
dbListTables(con)
```

# Count records in each database table

```{r}
dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT 'jobs' AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS records FROM jobs
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'skills', COUNT(*) FROM skills
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'job_skills', COUNT(*) FROM job_skills
")
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

I measured skill demand using the percentage of job postings requiring each skill.

```{r}
skill_demand <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    s.skill_name,
    COUNT(js.job_id) AS job_count
  FROM skills s
  LEFT JOIN job_skills js ON s.skill_id = js.skill_id
  GROUP BY s.skill_id, s.skill_name
  ORDER BY job_count DESC
") |>
  mutate(
    percentage = round(100 * job_count / nrow(jobs), 1)
  )

knitr::kable(skill_demand)
```

## Most Requested Skills

```{r}
ggplot(skill_demand,
       aes(x = reorder(skill_name, percentage),
           y = percentage)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#168C91") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Requested Data Science Skills",
    x = "Technical Skill",
    y = "Percentage of Job Postings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Skill Demand by Job Title

```{r}
job_comparison <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
    j.job_title,
    s.skill_name,
    COUNT(DISTINCT js.job_id) AS skill_count
  FROM jobs j
  JOIN job_skills js ON j.job_id = js.job_id
  JOIN skills s ON js.skill_id = s.skill_id
  GROUP BY j.job_title, s.skill_name
") |>
  left_join(
    jobs |> count(job_title, name = "total_jobs"),
    by = "job_title"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    percentage = round(100 * skill_count / total_jobs, 1)
  )

ggplot(job_comparison,
       aes(x = skill_name, y = percentage,
           fill = job_title)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Skill Demand Across Job Categories",
    x = "Technical Skill",
    y = "Percentage of Job Postings",
    fill = "Job Title"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Data Quality Checks

```{r}
# Missing values in each column
missing_summary <- jobs_raw |>
  summarise(across(
    everything(),
    ~ sum(is.na(.x))
  )) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "column",
    values_to = "missing_count"
  )

knitr::kable(missing_summary)

# Identify duplicate job IDs
sum(duplicated(jobs_raw$job_id))

# Check salary distribution and potential outliers
summary(jobs_raw$salary)

ggplot(jobs_raw, aes(x = salary)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#168C91") +
  labs(
    title = "Salary Distribution and Potential Outliers",
    x = "Salary (units as reported in source)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Conclusion

The analysis examined `r nrow(jobs)` job postings and five technical skills. The most frequently requested skill was **`r skill_demand$skill_name[1]`**, appearing in **`r skill_demand$percentage[1]`%** of postings. The second most common skill was **`r skill_demand$skill_name[2]`**, appearing in **`r skill_demand$percentage[2]`%** of postings.

The comparison across job titles illustrates how technical skill requirements vary between positions. These results provide an indication of employer demand, but the dataset includes only five skill categories and may not represent the entire job market.

The analysis is exploratory, and skill frequency does not necessarily measure the economic value or importance of a skill.
